solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A walk in the park with a hunk from Madeira?

definitions.meaning: an idiom for something very easy to do
a chunk cut from a Madeira, a plain British sponge loaf

explanation.surface: A stroll in a park, perhaps on the Portuguese island of Madeira, with a handsome man in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: Madeira looks like the island and the hunk like a muscular man; in fact Madeira is a type of sponge cake, and a hunk of it is a slice.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms for a task needing no effort, and the second is also literally a slice of sponge.

clue.text: Orchestra's appearance among islands is a loser

indicators.note: among means set inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: the Aran Islands lie off the west coast of Ireland
LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra

explanation.surface: An orchestra's island tour flops.
explanation.walkthrough: The LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra; ARAN is the group of Irish islands.
explanation.definitionFit: An unplaced runner in a race, and so anyone who fails to win, is called this.

clue.text: Setter's embracing Mum — he's good at supplication!

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself: 'setter is' gives I'M
Ma is another word for mother

explanation.surface: The puzzle-maker hugs his mother and prays well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' stands for 'the setter is', in his own words I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muslim prayer leader, who leads the congregation in worship, is fairly described as skilled at prayer.

clue.text: McPhee — ever young — regularly gets mark for service

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: An ageless man called McPhee wins a service medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes every second letter of 'McPhee ever young'.
explanation.definitionFit: A V-shaped stripe on a uniform sleeve shows rank or length of service.

clue.text: Satellite broadcast aberration cut off early with areas missed

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the remaining letters are strewn into a new order
missed means left out, so both of those letters are dropped
the word is cut off before its end, so its final letter goes

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area, so two areas are two As

explanation.surface: A satellite broadcast fault: the transmission was cut off early and some regions missed it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut off early' drops the last letter, N, of ABERRATION, and 'with areas missed' removes its two As, leaving BERRTIO for 'broadcast' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A spacecraft that circles a planet rather than landing on it is an artificial satellite.

clue.text: Blackguards — little short of evil

indicators.note: falling a little short means the last letter is missing

parts.note: a curse is an evil or affliction

explanation.surface: Scoundrels who are very nearly evil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little short of' looks like 'almost' but drops the last letter of CURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cur is a contemptible man, a scoundrel, so the plural matches blackguards.

clue.text: Cloaks behind under kimono initially, then sunbathes topless

indicators.note: in a down clue being under places this piece after the one above
initially means at the start, so the word's opening letter is taken

parts.note: aft means at the back, behind

indicators.note: topless means without the top, so the first letter goes

parts.note: someone who sunbathes tans

explanation.surface: Robes, kimonos at first, then someone sunbathing topless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' looks like a sunbather with no top but drops the T of TANS.
explanation.definitionFit: These are long loose tunics or robes, close enough to loose outer garments such as cloaks.

clue.text: Dirty work, but employment for stand-up, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the trade of a comedian: comic business

explanation.surface: Shady dealing, though a comic could call it his job.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase literally: comedy is a comic's line of work.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means trickery or deceit, and read literally it is the trade of being funny.

clue.text: Dot's type of engine used for internet site

parts.note: a bullet is a dot marking a list item
an inboard engine is mounted inside a boat's hull

explanation.surface: Someone called Dot asks what engine a website uses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dot' looks like a name or a full stop; here it is a bullet point. An INBOARD is a motor fixed inside a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: An online forum where users post messages is named after the physical noticeboard.

clue.text: Put to shame, e.g. at spud-bashing? There's some left!

indicators.note: in an across clue going left means the run is read backwards, right to left
some of the letters, so a run is lifted from inside the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone shamed while peeling potatoes, with some spuds still to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes EGATSPU from 'e.g. at spud', and 'left' turns it round. 'Spud-bashing' is army slang for peeling potatoes, a punishment duty.
explanation.definitionFit: To upstage someone is to outshine them and draw attention away, which shows them up.

clue.text: Flier reportedly did what he could for infection

parts.note: a bird is something that flies

indicators.note: says that the word for the next phrase is heard rather than written as it sounds

parts.note: what a bird can do is fly, so in the past tense he flew

explanation.surface: A pilot did all he could, so we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot, but it is the bird; 'reportedly' turns FLEW into the identical-sounding FLU.
explanation.definitionFit: Avian influenza, commonly called by this name, is a viral illness of poultry that can pass to people.

clue.text: Wind up in grass

explanation.surface: Something ending up lying in the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are British slang: as a verb it means annoy, and as a noun it is a police informer, also called a grass.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses the one word both for irritating someone and for a person who informs to the police.

clue.text: Starter with rosemary infusing each soup

indicators.note: infusing means steeping into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: both, as in 'they each have one', 'they both have one'

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its opening letter, here taken from the herb

explanation.surface: A cook's tip: begin by steeping rosemary in each soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' looks like the first course of a meal, but it means the first letter, R, which goes inside BOTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin soup made by simmering meat or vegetables in water is a classic example of the kind.

clue.text: Back storyteller's protest

indicators.note: back means the word is read the other way round

parts.note: a teller of stories, i.e. a fibber or liar

explanation.surface: Supporting an author's complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like 'support', but it is the reversal signal; a storyteller here is someone who tells fibs.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail against something is to complain about it bitterly, a verb sense of protest.

clue.text: Coaster breaks down following Queen Elizabeth sailing royal course

indicators.note: breaking down means falling apart, so the letters are reassembled
sailing means setting off and leaving, so those letters depart

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is her royal cipher

explanation.surface: A coastal ship breaks down after the liner Queen Elizabeth sails off on a royal voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen Elizabeth sailing' suggests the liner but means ER leaving COASTER; 'breaks down' rearranges COAST.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse in Berkshire hosts Royal Ascot, the summer meeting attended by the monarch.

clue.text: Leading lady from the south eating duck — duck!

indicators.note: eating means taking in, so one piece holds the other
in a down clue read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a diva is a leading female singer
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A prima donna dining on duck, then a warning to take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the south' turns DIVA upwards into AVID, and 'eating' puts O inside. A duck is a cricket score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck a blow or a question is to dodge or evade it.

clue.text: No need for hospital with bruised shinbone — that's a blessing

indicators.note: says one letter of the bruised word is not needed and drops out
bruising damages the shape, so the leg-bone word is battered into new order

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A battered shin, luckily not bad enough to need hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Take H from SHINBONE and rearrange the other letters, as 'No need for' and 'bruised' say.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a blessing or benediction, used poetically.

clue.text: Take another look at increase in speed; could it be …

parts.note: to rev is to increase an engine's speed
the question 'could it be?' can be put as 'is it?'

explanation.surface: A driver puts his foot down, wondering whether it could be the next clue's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links into the next clue but is only surface; 'could it be' gives IS IT as a question.
explanation.definitionFit: To revisit something is to go back to it and consider it again.

clue.text: … carbohydrate source's involved?

indicators.note: involved means tangled or complicated, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: could a carbohydrate source be involved?
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' scrambles the letters of SOURCE'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Table sugar is a disaccharide, one of the commonest carbohydrates in the diet.

clue.text: Plant that's successful in fall

definitions.meaning: a plant that yields well, a good producer
a heavy fall, as in 'to come a ...'

explanation.surface: A plant that does well in autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall' looks like autumn, as in American English, but is a tumble; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant judged by its yield is called a good or poor one, and the idiom 'come a ...' means fall heavily.

clue.text: This offender gets proposal

parts.note: swap the answer in for 'This': the word 'offender' with the three letters E, N, D removed from its middle gets you 'offer', a proposal

explanation.surface: A criminal receives an offer.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: put the answer in place of 'This' and the clue reads as an instruction, turning OFFENDER into OFFER.
explanation.definitionFit: The solution stands in for 'This', acting as the instruction that deletes three letters from the wrongdoer.

clue.text: Brace of snipe's capital, pet — finish shortly

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first, capital letter

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulking, as is a tiff

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the finish is the end

explanation.surface: A shooting scene: two snipe, a sulk and a quick end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brace of snipe' suggests a pair of game birds, but 'Brace' is the definition and 'of' a link. 'shortly' trims END to EN.
explanation.definitionFit: To brace something is to make it firm or rigid, so it is a synonymous verb.

clue.text: Rest of junk below bottom of stairs

indicators.note: in a down clue being below puts this piece after the one above
in a down clue the bottom of a word is its final letter

parts.note: lumber is unwanted junk stored away

explanation.surface: The rest of the junk is stored under the stairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' looks like 'the remainder' but is the definition, sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleep, which is a form of rest, is a synonym here.

clue.text: Works discovered 'online'?

parts.note: found means discovered
read as 'on line': placed on RY, the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Something found on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'online' looks like the internet, but split it as 'on line': in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the abbreviation for railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A metal-casting factory is a type of works, as in ironworks.

clue.text: Den staying in, correct?

parts.note: a batsman still in is 'not out', abbreviated NO on a cricket scorecard
OK means all right or correct

explanation.surface: Is staying at home in the den the right thing to do?
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman staying in is 'not out', shown as NO on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are small secluded spaces or corners where someone can retreat.

clue.text: Blame rostrum after Penny tumbles

indicators.note: Penny tumbles off the platform, so that letter falls away

parts.note: a podium is a raised platform for a speaker
P is the abbreviation for a penny in British money

explanation.surface: Someone is blamed for the stage collapsing after Penny falls off it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a woman's name, but it is P, which 'tumbles' off PODIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium means general hatred or disgrace attaching to someone, close to blame or opprobrium.

clue.text: Victor's skirt — ordinary?

definitions.note: the surname belonging to Victor, the French writer of Les Misérables

parts.note: to skirt a coast is to hug it, keeping close
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, from old O-level exams

explanation.surface: Asking whether Victor's skirt is a plain, ordinary one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirt' looks like a garment, but as a verb it means to keep close to, as a ship hugs the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist Victor bore this surname, so the possessive points to his family name.

clue.text: Penultimate contest ends in trouble — players held up on motorway

indicators.note: in a down clue held up means turned upwards, read backwards
the ends of the two words are their final letters

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI

explanation.surface: A semi-final hit by trouble as the team are stuck in motorway traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends in' picks E and S from 'trouble' and 'players'; 'held up' reverses them to SE. The M1 runs from London to Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: The round before the final is short for semi-final.

clue.text: Head pedicab off with crazy bid to escape

indicators.note: off means wrong or disordered, so the cab's letters are reordered
crazy says the letters of the bid are scattered in the cab, not in a row
the letters of the bid get away from the cab's letters; that the answer's letters also sit inside 'escape' is a coincidence

explanation.surface: A cycle-rickshaw rider makes a mad attempt to get away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a verb but is a headland. 'off' scrambles PEDICAB less B, I and D, which 'crazy bid to escape' removes.
explanation.definitionFit: A promontory such as the Cape of Good Hope is also called a head or headland.

clue.text: Sovereign to dine with army unit

parts.note: to sup is to eat supper
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers of the British Army

explanation.surface: A monarch is to dine with a regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the British Army's corps of Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, sovereign means highest in rank or authority, a synonym.

clue.text: Bishop left calculator in bag

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
an adder is something that adds up figures

explanation.surface: A bishop left his pocket calculator in his bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calculator' is a machine in the surface; here it is anything that adds, an ADDER.
explanation.definitionFit: An anatomical sac that holds urine or a football's inflatable inner is a kind of bag.

clue.text: If wearing ruby earrings is 1ac, it's not this!

definitions.text: If wearing ruby earrings is 1ac, it's not this!

indicators.note: wearing suggests wearing away or wearing down, so the letters are worn into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Putting on ruby earrings is easy, hardly a skilled operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' looks like putting on jewellery but reworks RUBY EARRINGS. The whole clue echoes the saying 'it's not rocket science', with 1ac meaning easy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'it's not neurosurgery' is said of any task that is easy, the opposite of a difficult operation.
